subject: GenSA vs Optimx after update to BioGeoBEARS 1.1

messages.author: d7fd273d0b8c973d
messages.subject: GenSA vs Optimx after update to BioGeoBEARS 1.1
parts:
Hello Nick and all users,

I am running a bunch of additional runs using the different models (divalike, bayarea, dec) and their j variations on my data set to further conduce AIC tests and all that jazz.

Everything seems to be working fine so far, after the update. I haven't got any error messages or anything like that.

I have two questions that are more about my curiosity:

1. I have been noticing a considerable slowdown on the speeds of execution of BioGeoBears. My DEC and DECJ runs that I set before the update have been running for a while, using optimx. I had a divalike and a baylike that took almost  a month to finish, when previously they were finishing in around a week or 10 days. Have anyone else noticed something like this?

2. The divalike+j and baylike+j runs were set to execute a couple of days ago, but this time using the GenSA option instead of the optimx, as advised in this group. I am using the results from the previous divalike and bayarealike runs, also following the recommended script provided by Nick. These two runs are going SLOW. Very few screen updates. When the run starts we all get a warning message that GenSA might be faster or slower. Just wanted to know if any one else is facing an apparent slowdown using GenSA compared to optimx.

Cheers

JP

Hi!  Thanks for the question.  I'll give you my sense of all this, which hopefully will help:

1. It looks like both optimx and GenSA work fine, without crashing, if these have all been updated to the new versions: 
- R itself
- rexpokit (0.15 from CRAN)
- cladoRcpp (0.26.6 from CRAN)
- BioGeoBEARS (version 1.1 from GitHub).

So: you should be able to use either one.



2. You may get a speedup if you "byte-compile" the BioGeoBEARS package when installing from GitHub -- this might be a speedup of a few times.  Byte-compilation is default from CRAN packages, but perhaps not from GitHub, I'm not sure.  I haven't tested the speed, but the installation from GitHub works with byte-compilation on:

library(devtools)
devtools::install_github(repo="nmatzke/BioGeoBEARS", INSTALL_opts="--byte-compile")



3. Also: especially for GenSA, it is useful to have the on_NaN_error option set, like this:

BioGeoBEARS_run_object$on_NaN_error = -1e50

...this means that, if a parameter combination is tried that results in a NaN for the likelihood (usually parameters at the very edges of the parameter limits), instead of returning NaN and crashing the search, instead a lnL of -1e50 is returned, and the search continues.

A few days ago I made this the default setting in 1.1.  This is more important in GenSA, since GenSA does a more thorough search and seems to explore the boundaries of the parameter space as part of this.


4. GenSA definitely takes several times longer than optimx to optimize.  It is doing a more thorough search (in my experience), and so it calculates the likelihood more times.  The benefit of this is that there is a lower chance of find a claimed Maximum Likelihood result that is actually just a local optimum, instead of a global optimum.  My experience is that this is important e.g. in trait-dependent dispersal models (where you have e.g. 6 or 7 free parameters), but not really for the standard DEC vs DEC+J problems with 2 or 3 parameters.  Detailed advice on thinking about your optimization results, and ways to check, here:

Issues with Maximum Likelihood (ML) optimization
http://phylo.wikidot.com/biogeobears-mistakes-to-avoid#optim



5. The choice of optimx versus GenSA should not effect the length of individual likelihood calculations, ie individual steps in the ML search.  These should stay the same either way.  What makes GenSA slower is that it is doing more likelihood calculations during the search.


6. The slow step in the likelihood calculation is matrix exponentiation. These are done by rexpokit, which wraps the FORTRAN code EXPOKIT.  As far as I know, this should not have gotten slower in the update -- but, CRAN forced me to make some minor changes to the EXPOKIT source code in order to pass CRAN's checks, and it is vaguely possible (but doesn't seem likely to me) that this could have made the code less efficient.  If people keep seeing this, let me know.


7. One thing that would definitely slow down the likelihood calculations, for large problems, is if parallelization was unavailable on a particular setup (e.g. only 1 core available, R.app only runs on 1 core, etc.).  But, BioGeoBEARS should report how many cores are available and how many are being used.


Cheers!
Nick
